headline: An ad about love upsets the internet

sources.title: 'You literally can't': AI startup Orchid sparks backlash over its 'second brain' assistant
Orchid AI assistant launches, gets backlash for relationship ad
'Tech people need to stop': Startup faces backlash after suggesting its AI can save bad relationships

chunks.text: An argument {{kicked off}} on July 28, when a short [[advertisement]] for an AI [[assistant]] called Orchid appeared online. The app works [[by text message]] and {{sorts out}} small jobs: [[bookings]], [[reminders]], files. In the [[clip]], a man forgets his [[anniversary]] while he is playing a video game. His partner messages the assistant instead of him, and the assistant {{stands in for}} him by handling the conversation. It books a restaurant and sends lilies, because it remembers that she likes them better than roses.

verbs.wrong: To end a video with a joke
verbs.why: A loud argument can kick off after just one careless comment, and a new sports season kicks off every fall with high hopes. An online argument kicked off on July 28 when a short ad for the AI assistant Orchid appeared.

verbs.wrong: To reply to a message very fast
verbs.why: An assistant might sort out your schedule before a busy week, and a good manager sorts out small problems before they grow. The Orchid app sorts out small jobs like bookings, reminders, and files through text messages.

verbs.correct: To do something in place of someone
verbs.wrong: To send flowers to a partner
verbs.why: A backup actor stands in for the lead when she gets sick, and a backup singer sometimes stands in for the star at the last minute. In the ad, the assistant stands in for the man by handling all of his partner's messages.

chunks.text: The video {{blew up}}. It reached 3.2 million [[views]] and more than 600 [[replies]] [[in a few days]]. Many people who had been [[ready to]] {{sign up}} {{turned on}} the company instead. The line that made people angriest was the assistant's own: "You literally can't. [[That's why]] I'm here." Its [[critics]] said the app was selling a way to look [[thoughtful]] without doing any of the caring.

verbs.correct: To suddenly get a lot of attention
verbs.wrong: To delete a post after an argument
verbs.why: A funny video can blow up online within hours, and one lucky post might blow up overnight after a celebrity shares it. This ad blew up fast, reaching 3.2 million views and more than 600 replies in just a few days.

verbs.correct: To join a service as a member
verbs.wrong: To book a table at a restaurant
verbs.why: Students sign up for a free workshop within minutes of it opening, and a new member can sign up for the gym online in seconds. Many people who had planned to sign up for Orchid criticized the company instead after seeing the ad.

verbs.wrong: To share a video with a friend
verbs.why: Fans quickly turn on a coach after a bad losing streak, and a crowd can turn on a referee after one unfair call. Many people who once liked Orchid turned on the company after this advertisement appeared online.

chunks.text: A [[licensed therapist]] {{spoke out}} too. She warned that texting a machine instead of your partner is [[a form of]] [[triangulation]]: a third person {{cuts in}} on a conversation that should happen only between the two partners. Some readers said [[the whole thing]] {{put off}} people who had planned to try the app. Others called it [[ragebait]], made to be shared in anger.

verbs.correct: To say publicly what you think
verbs.wrong: To answer a message in private
verbs.why: Employees sometimes speak out against a rule they think is unfair, and worried parents speak out at a school board meeting. A licensed therapist spoke out too, warning that texting an assistant instead of a partner can hurt real communication.

verbs.correct: To interrupt and take a place
verbs.wrong: To lower the price of an app
verbs.why: A stranger sometimes cuts in during a private conversation at a party, and a rude driver might cut in front of others on the highway. The therapist warned that a machine can cut in on a conversation that should stay strictly between two partners.

verbs.wrong: To remind someone of a date
verbs.why: Bad reviews put off many potential buyers before they even visit a store, and rude service can put off even loyal customers for good. Some readers said the whole argument put off people who had once planned to try the Orchid app.

chunks.text: The company has not {{backed down}}. It said it wanted a story built around a real situation [[rather than]] a normal product video, and it {{brushed off}} the criticism by leaving the clip online. A second advertisement, which claimed the app could check food for [[allergens]], was quietly deleted. The fight {{sums up}} a question the [[tech industry]] keeps [[running into]]: people will let software book a table, but they do not want it to do the caring for them.

verbs.wrong: To repeat a claim more loudly
verbs.why: A union refuses to back down during a long, difficult strike, and some companies back down fast once bad press starts to spread. Orchid has not backed down, and it left the anniversary ad online rather than removing it.

verbs.wrong: To delete a video from the internet
verbs.why: A driver might brush off a warning light and keep driving anyway, and some workers brush off small rumors around the office. Orchid brushed off the criticism and simply left the ad online for anyone to see.

verbs.correct: To capture the whole of something
verbs.wrong: To start a new argument online
verbs.why: One photo can sum up an entire vacation better than any story, and a single quote sometimes sums up a whole argument. This fight sums up a real tension in tech: people accept an app booking a table but not doing their emotional work.

mainIdea.s: An advertisement for an AI assistant called Orchid showed it standing in for a man who forgot his anniversary. The clip caused a huge backlash, and critics said it sold care without real caring.
mainIdea.why: The ad reached 3.2 million views and heavy backlash after critics said the assistant was selling a way to look thoughtful without any real caring.

mainIdea.s: The company quickly deleted the anniversary advertisement after a licensed therapist spoke out against it. Orchid then apologized and promised to build its next ad around a happier couple.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the company did not delete the anniversary ad or apologize. It left the clip online and quietly removed a different ad about food allergens instead.

mainIdea.s: A separate AI company this year launched a chatbot that helps couples plan a wedding budget together. The tool books venues and tracks costs, but it does not send messages for either partner.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a different AI chatbot built for wedding planning, not about the Orchid anniversary advertisement.

lines.text: An ad for an AI assistant made the whole internet angry this week.

A man forgets his anniversary while playing a video game. His partner messages his AI assistant instead of him, and the assistant {{stands in for}} him: books a restaurant, sends her favorite flowers, handles the whole conversation.
[[Oof]]. And people saw this as a good thing?

The company did. The internet didn't. The video {{blew up}}: 3.2 million views and hundreds of angry replies. The argument {{kicked off}} over one line from the assistant itself: "You literally can't. That's why I'm here."
Meaning the man literally can't care?
[[That's how people read it]]. Critics said the app was selling a way to look thoughtful without doing any of the caring. People who had been ready to {{sign up}} {{turned on}} the company instead.
One {{spoke out}} and called it triangulation: a third party {{cuts in}} on a conversation that should happen only between partners.
No, it hasn't {{backed down}}. It said it wanted a story around a real situation, and it {{brushed off}} the criticism by leaving the clip online. A second ad was quietly deleted, though.
What does the app even do normally?
Ordinary useful things. It works by text and {{sorts out}} small jobs: bookings, reminders, files. Some readers said the ad {{put off}} exactly the people who wanted that.
So the ad {{sums up}} a bigger question.
[[Perfectly]]. People will let software book a table, but they don't want it to do the caring for them.
The restaurant, yes. The flowers... [[that's a line you don't cross]].

expressions.def: An informal reaction to something painful or embarrassing
ex: He sent the email to the whole company. Oof.

expressions.def: That is how people understood it
ex: She meant it as a joke, but that's not how people read it.

expressions.def: A one-word way to say "exactly right"
ex: Does that describe him? Perfectly.

expressions.expr: that's a line you don't cross
expressions.def: A limit that must be respected
ex: Reading someone's diary? That's a line you don't cross.
